docs.title: Reference implementation
docs.text:
Ory Kratos (commit b86338d) is the identity server. It runs the registration flow, checks the input, and stores identities and sessions. The UI is a separate web app that only renders the forms Kratos describes.

  • Kratos (public API): http://127.0.0.1:4433
  • UI: http://127.0.0.1:4455

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Browser opens the sign-up page: GET :4455/registration.
  2. UI has no flow yet, so it redirects the browser to Kratos to start one: GET :4433/self-service/registration/browser.
  3. Kratos creates a registration flow, sets a CSRF cookie, and redirects back to the UI with the flow ID: /registration?flow=<id>.

  4. UI fetches the flow from Kratos (GET /self-service/registration/flows?id=<id>) and shows the profile form. The flow describes the form (server-driven UI, trimmed):

    {
  "id": "faaa3fc0-0203-4085-ac76-3b6ca668908a",
  "type": "browser",
  "state": "choose_method",
  "expires_at": "2026-10-12T01:10:49Z",
  "ui": {
    "action": "http://127.0.0.1:4433/self-service/registration?flow=faaa3fc0-…",
    "method": "POST",
    "nodes": [
      { "attributes": { "name": "csrf_token", "type": "hidden", "value": "<token>" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.email", "type": "email", "required": true } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.first", "type": "text" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.last", "type": "text" } },
      { "attributes": { "name": "method", "type": "submit", "value": "profile" } }
    ]
  }
}

  5. Browser submits the profile to Kratos: POST /self-service/registration?flow=<id>.

    Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

csrf_token=<token>
&traits.email=test@test.com
&traits.name.first=Test1
&traits.name.last=Test
&method=profile

  6. Kratos checks the profile, then changes the form stored in the flow for the next screen: the profile fields become hidden and a password field is added. It redirects back to the UI: /registration?flow=<id>. No account is created yet. Answering a form post with a redirect is the Post/Redirect/Get pattern, so a page refresh does not resubmit the form.

  7. UI fetches the flow again and shows the password form. The profile values are now hidden fields:

    "nodes": [
  { "attributes": { "name": "csrf_token", "type": "hidden", "value": "<token>" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.email", "type": "hidden", "value": "test@test.com" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.first", "type": "hidden", "value": "Test1" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "traits.name.last", "type": "hidden", "value": "Test" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "password", "type": "password", "required": true } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "method", "type": "submit", "value": "password" } },
  { "attributes": { "name": "screen", "type": "submit", "value": "previous" } }
]

  8. Browser submits the password to Kratos, with the profile again: POST /self-service/registration?flow=<id>.

    csrf_token=<token>
&traits.email=test@test.com
&traits.name.first=Test1
&traits.name.last=Test
&password=<password>
&method=password

  9. Kratos checks the input, creates the identity and a session, starts email verification, and redirects (303 See Other) to the UI's verification page with the session cookie:

    HTTP/1.1 303 See Other
Location: http://127.0.0.1:4455/verification?flow=2f6c3de3-1d88-4dfd-916b-fedc463f39f7
Set-Cookie: ory_kratos_session=<session>; …

  10. UI shows the verification form. The user is now logged in.

docs.title: Server-driven UI
docs.text:
Kratos decides what the form contains, and the UI only draws it. Each flow carries ui.nodes (UI nodes), a list of fields with name, type, required flag, value and error messages, plus ui.action and ui.method for where to post. The UI loops over the nodes and renders them. It controls only layout and styling.

This keeps the rules in one place. A new trait in the identity schema (a JSON Schema), or a new method such as passkeys, shows up in every UI without UI changes. Web, mobile and single-page apps render the same nodes. Kratos checks every submit against the flow it stored, so a client cannot skip a step. Errors come back as the same flow with messages on the fields. The cost is flexibility: a fully custom sign-up sequence is harder, because Kratos decides the steps.

docs.title: CSRF
docs.text:
Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is when another site makes the user's browser send a request the user did not intend. Without protection, another site could post a sign-up form to Kratos from the user's browser. The browser would follow the redirect and store the session cookie, so the user would be logged in to an account the attacker created and controls. Anything the user then enters goes into the attacker's account. This is called login CSRF.

To block this, Kratos requires a secret that only the user's browser holds, and checks that every form post carries it. This is the double-submit cookie pattern:

  • Secret. On the first request from a browser with no CSRF cookie (step 3, GET /self-service/registration/browser), Kratos generates a random secret and stores it in an HttpOnly cookie named csrf_token_<hash>. It is one secret per browser, kept across flows.
  • Form field. Whenever Kratos builds a form (step 3, and again in step 6), it puts a copy of the secret in the hidden csrf_token field. The copy is masked with fresh random bytes each time, which is why the field value differs between steps 5 and 8. Masking protects against BREACH, an attack that recovers a secret repeated unchanged in compressed HTTPS responses.
  • Check. On each submit (steps 5 and 8), Kratos unmasks the field and compares it with the cookie. If they don't match, the post is rejected.

Another site can make the browser send the cookie, but the same-origin policy stops it from reading the cookie or the form, so it cannot fill in the field.

API flows for native apps use no cookies, so they skip this check. Instead, Kratos rejects an API flow request that carries cookies or an Origin header, since that means it came from a browser.

docs.title: Have I Been Pwned
docs.text:
Kratos rejects passwords that have already leaked in a data breach, because attackers try those first, for example in credential stuffing. NIST SP 800-63B-4 §3.1.1.2 requires this: a new password SHALL be compared against a blocklist that includes passwords from previous breaches. Kratos asks Have I Been Pwned (HIBP), using its Pwned Passwords API, without ever sending the password: it asks for a bucket of leaked passwords that look alike, then searches the bucket itself.

This runs on the password submit (step 8), after the length check (at least 8 characters) and a check that the password is not too similar to the email (by Levenshtein distance and longest common substring):

  1. Kratos hashes the password with SHA-1. password becomes 5BAA61E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8.
  2. It sends only the first 5 characters: GET https://api.pwnedpasswords.com/range/5BAA6.
  3. HIBP returns every leaked hash starting with that prefix, as suffix and count. For 5BAA6, that was 1,977 lines on 2026-10-11, including 1E4C9B93F3F0682250B6CF8331B7EE68FD8:52372427.
  4. Kratos looks for its own suffix in the list. If the count is above max_breaches (default 0), the password is rejected with an error on the password field.

Hundreds of passwords share each prefix, so HIBP cannot tell which one was checked. This technique is called k-anonymity; Cloudflare describes its design for HIBP. SHA-1 is used only because the HIBP dataset is indexed by it; the stored password is hashed separately with bcrypt. If HIBP is unreachable, Kratos accepts the password (ignore_network_errors defaults to true). This is a fail-open choice: an outage does not block sign-ups, but the leak check is skipped.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Five tables in three groups:

  • The person: identities.
  • How they prove it: identity_credentials holds the secret, and identity_credential_identifiers holds what the user types to find it.
  • Short-lived state: registration_flows for a sign-up in progress, and sessions for a logged-in device.
erDiagram
    identities ||--o{ identity_credentials : "proves with"
    identity_credentials ||--|{ identity_credential_identifiers : "found by"
    identities ||--o{ sessions : "logged in as"
  • identities 1:M identity_credentials: an identity has zero or more credentials, at most one per type.
  • identity_credentials 1:M identity_credential_identifiers: a credential has one or more identifiers.
  • identities 1:M sessions: an identity has zero or more sessions, one per logged-in device.
  • registration_flows stands alone: a flow exists before any identity does.

Every table uses a UUIDv7 primary key, generated by PostgreSQL 18 with uuidv7(). The IDs are unguessable but time-ordered, so new rows append to the index like a sequence. IDs are never used as secrets.

All times are timestamptz, so the server's time zone cannot change what is stored.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text: The examples follow Ada, who signs up with Ada@Example.com.

docs.title: identities
docs.text:
One row per person. Everything else points to it.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK traits jsonb Profile: email, first_name, last_name created_at, updated_at timestamptz

Example:

id traits 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc {"email": "Ada@Example.com", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace"}

There is deliberately no unique constraint on traits.email. The profile keeps the email as typed. What must be unique is the login identifier, enforced in identity_credential_identifiers.

docs.title: identity_credentials
docs.text:
One row per way the person can prove who they are: password now, passkeys or social sign-in later. A new login method is a new row, not a new column.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK identity_id uuid → identities, cascade delete type text, checked Login method, such as password; later webauthn or oidc config jsonb Method-specific data, such as the password hash created_at, updated_at timestamptz

Example:

id identity_id type config 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc password {"hashed_password": "$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$…"}

Constraints:

  • FOREIGN KEY (identity_id) → identities, cascade delete. A credential must belong to a real identity. A password credential for identity 01a12be8-3280-7c45-81ad-1c992c1aa770, which does not exist, is rejected. Deleting Ada's identity deletes her password credential with it, so no password is left behind for an account that is gone.
  • CHECK (type IN ('password')). Only known methods. A row with type pasword is rejected instead of becoming a credential no login code ever reads.
  • UNIQUE (identity_id, type). At most one credential per method. A second password row for identity 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc is rejected; otherwise login would not know which of Ada's two hashes to check.
  • UNIQUE (id, type). Needed only for the foreign key from identity_credential_identifiers. Postgres requires a foreign key to point at columns with a unique constraint.

The password hash is stored in PHC string format. The algorithm and its parameters travel with the hash, so they can be raised later and old hashes upgraded at the next login. Argon2id is the first choice in the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: identity_credential_identifiers
docs.text:
What the user types to find a credential at login, such as their email. The credential is the lock; the identifier says which lock to try. It is a separate table because one credential can have several identifiers, for example a password usable with either an email or a username.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK credential_id uuid The credential this identifier finds type text Login method of the credential, such as password; part of the unique key identifier text What the user types at login, such as ada@example.com; trimmed and lowercased for emails

Example:

id credential_id type identifier 01a12be9-a59a-715f-9320-76c6be463887 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d password ada@example.com

Constraints:

  • UNIQUE (type, identifier). One account per login. When someone else signs up with ada@example.com, inserting (password, ada@example.com) fails with Postgres error 23505 (unique_violation). This is what stops duplicate sign-ups. A passkey row (webauthn, ada@example.com) is still allowed, because uniqueness is per method.
  • FOREIGN KEY (credential_id, type) → identity_credentials (id, type), cascade delete. The identifier must point at a real credential of the same method. An identifier with credential 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d and type oidc is rejected, because that credential's type is password. Deleting the credential deletes its identifier, so the email can be used to sign up again.

type is copied into this table because a unique constraint can only cover columns of one table. The composite foreign key is what keeps the copy honest.

Normalization happens before insert, and the rule depends on the method. For password login, emails are trimmed and lowercased, so Ada@Example.com is stored as ada@example.com and ADA@example.com hits the unique constraint. A social sign-in subject ID is case-sensitive and kept as is.

docs.title: sessions
docs.text:
One row per logged-in device. Logging out one device does not touch the others.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK token_hash bytea, unique SHA-256 of the cookie token identity_id uuid → identities, cascade delete Indexed active boolean Set to false on logout authenticated_at, issued_at, expires_at timestamptz

Example, Ada on her laptop and phone, after logging out the phone:

id token_hash identity_id active expires_at 01a12be9-a59b-7960-b916-09ef91f6ffd0 \xca89d7ee0f5c7bdcf54ef44ed4bd7178bd9b61f830f0955e9d4a6e4f0ff14436 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc true 2026-10-12 10:00 01a12c1f-2100-7259-8053-8c6eb59da032 \x05942f4bfc35d135c2174cd6cbc0441b8719b2701da3fa984524214527b8d19a 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc false 2026-10-12 11:00

Constraints:

  • UNIQUE (token_hash). A cookie must lead to exactly one session. A second row with the same hash is rejected, so a lookup by cookie can never return someone else's session.
  • FOREIGN KEY (identity_id) → identities, cascade delete. A session for a missing identity is rejected. Deleting Ada's identity deletes both sessions, which logs her out everywhere.

The cookie carries a random 32-byte token, and the table stores only its hash, so a database leak gives no usable sessions. A fast hash is enough here, unlike for passwords, because the token is fully random and cannot be guessed. See the OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet.

identity_id also needs its own index. Postgres does not index foreign key columns automatically, and without it, listing Ada's sessions or deleting her identity scans the whole table.

docs.title: registration_flows
docs.text:
One row per sign-up attempt. It keeps what the user typed and the errors until they succeed, without creating an account.

Column Type Notes id uuid PK csrf_token text Ties the flow to the browser that started it state jsonb Submitted values (never the password) and errors per field expires_at timestamptz Rejected after this; deleted later created_at, updated_at timestamptz

Example, after Ada's first attempt with a password that is too short:

id state expires_at 01a12be8-3280-760b-a59b-6095af80070a {"values": {"email": "Ada@Example.com", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace"}, "errors": {"password": "must be at least 8 characters"}} 2026-10-11 10:10

Constraints:

  • NOT NULL on expires_at and csrf_token. Every flow must expire and be tied to a browser. A flow without them is rejected, instead of living forever or being usable from any browser.
  • No foreign key to identities. A flow exists before any identity, and most flows never create one.

docs.title: Sign-up transaction
docs.text:
A successful sign-up creates four rows, and they must either all exist or none of them. So they are written in one transaction:

  1. identities: Ada's profile.

    id traits 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc {"email": "Ada@Example.com", "first_name": "Ada", "last_name": "Lovelace"}

  2. identity_credentials: her password hash.

    id identity_id type config 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc password {"hashed_password": "$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$…"}

  3. identity_credential_identifiers: her email for login.

    id credential_id type identifier 01a12be9-a59a-715f-9320-76c6be463887 01a12be9-a599-74c7-b7e6-70439cada89d password ada@example.com

  4. sessions: her laptop.

    id token_hash identity_id active expires_at 01a12be9-a59b-7960-b916-09ef91f6ffd0 \xca89d7ee0f5c7bdcf54ef44ed4bd7178bd9b61f830f0955e9d4a6e4f0ff14436 01a12be9-a598-707b-a6a3-1f96331092cc true 2026-10-12 10:00

Suppose the email is already taken. Steps 1 and 2 succeed, then step 3 is rejected by UNIQUE (type, identifier). Without a transaction, Ada's identity and password would stay in the database: an account with a password that nobody can log in to. With a transaction, Postgres undoes steps 1 and 2, and the database looks as if the sign-up never happened.

docs.title: PRECIS
docs.text: PRECIS is an IETF standard for checking whether two pieces of text, such as two usernames, should count as the same. The name stands for Preparation, Enforcement, and Comparison of Internationalized Strings.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
Text that looks the same to a person can be different bytes to a computer. Uppercase letters, fullwidth letters typed with an East Asian keyboard, and invisible characters copied along with pasted text all change the bytes but not what a person sees. If a login system compares names byte by byte, three things go wrong:

  • One person can create two accounts with the "same" email.
  • A user who signed up as Test@Example.com can't log in as test@example.com.
  • An attacker can register a copy of someone else's name that looks identical on screen.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• RFC 8264 defines the framework.
  • RFC 8265 applies it to usernames and passwords.
  • RFC 8266 applies it to nicknames (display names).

All three were published in 2017. They replace an older standard, Stringprep (RFC 3454).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
These inputs all look like the same email address. Here is what the PRECIS profile for usernames does with each:

Input Result test@example.com test@example.com Test@Example.com test@example.com ｔｅｓｔ@example.com (fullwidth) test@example.com test@example.com with a zero-width space after test Rejected

The first three become the same string, so they are the same account. The last one contains a character with no legitimate use in a name, so it is refused.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every string is turned into one standard form before it is stored or compared. A profile lists the steps: map fullwidth characters to normal ones, lowercase or keep case, apply Unicode normalization, then reject the string if any character is not allowed. Two strings are the same when their standard forms are identical.

RFC 8265 defines three profiles:

Profile For Case UsernameCaseMapped Usernames and emails Lowercased UsernameCasePreserved Case-sensitive usernames Kept OpaqueString Passwords Kept

Passwords keep their case, because lowercasing would make Secret and secret the same password.

The same profile has to run at sign-up and at login, or the stored name will never match what the user types. PRECIS also cannot catch letters from different alphabets that look alike, such as the Cyrillic а and the Latin a (RFC 8264, Section 12.5).

In Go, the profiles are in golang.org/x/text/secure/precis.

docs.title: Unicode normalization
docs.text: Unicode normalization is a set of standard rules for rewriting text into one agreed form, so that text which means the same thing is also stored as the same bytes. Unicode defines four of these forms: NFC, NFD, NFKC and NFKD.

docs.title: What problem it solves
docs.text:
Unicode often has more than one way to write the same character. é can be one code point (U+00E9), or the letter e followed by a combining accent (U+0301). Both display as é, but the bytes differ, so a program that compares bytes says they are not equal. Which form arrives depends on the device, the keyboard and the software that produced the text.

Without normalization:

  • The same name typed on two different machines may not match.
  • A search for café may miss a stored café.
  • One person can register the "same" account name twice.

docs.title: Where it is defined
docs.text:
• Unicode Standard Annex #15: Unicode Normalization Forms defines the four forms.
  • RFC 5198 asks internet protocols to exchange text in NFC.
  • PRECIS uses NFC as one step when comparing usernames and passwords.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Input NFC NFKC é as one code point (U+00E9) unchanged unchanged e + combining accent (U+0065 U+0301) é as one code point (U+00E9) é as one code point (U+00E9) ｔｅｓｔ (fullwidth) unchanged test ﬁle (with the ﬁ ligature) unchanged file x² unchanged x2

NFC makes the two spellings of é identical and leaves everything else alone. NFKC goes further and also folds lookalike variants into plain letters and digits.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The four forms come from two choices:

Composed (fewest code points) Decomposed (base letter + marks) Canonical: only characters that are truly the same NFC NFD Compatibility: also variants that look alike NFKC NFKD

Canonical forms never change meaning: the two kinds of é are the same character. Compatibility forms can lose information: x² becomes x2, which is no longer "x squared". This is why NFC is the usual choice, and why PRECIS uses NFC and handles fullwidth letters as a separate step.

Normalization only rewrites characters that Unicode considers equivalent. Invisible characters such as the zero-width space pass through unchanged, and so do letters from different alphabets that merely look alike, such as the Cyrillic а and the Latin a.

In Go, the forms are in golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm. Postgres has normalize(text, NFC) and the IS NFC NORMALIZED test (string functions).
